list.listitem: Diagnosis of arterial gas embolism is based on clinical history, with support from quantitative EEG, CT, MRI, and echocardiogram. C
The patient should be placed on supplemental oxygen in the supine position initially, then treated with hyperbaric oxygen as soon as the patient is hemodynamically stable. C
A significant number of patients will experience residual neurologic deficits from cerebral air embolism. C

background.definition: Arterial gas embolism results from the entry of gas into the pulmonary veins or directly into the systemic arterial circulation. It is a rare, life-threatening entity requiring high clinical index of suspicion and early intervention. Even with a small amount of gas in the arterial sytem, the gas bubbles can flow into the functional end arteries occluding these vessels. The occlusion of end-arteries is possible in any arteries, but is especially serious and may prove fatal with involvement of coronary or cerebral arteries.

list.listitem: The frequency of venous air embolization following placement of central venous access is less than 2%; arterial gas embolism is less common in comparison.
The entry of gas/air into the arterial circulation is rare, as the high pressure system in the arterial circulation is relatively protective from the entry of gas compared to the venous system.

The true incidence of cerebral arterial gas embolism is unknown. A prospective cohort study at a French hospital found 125 proven cases of iatrogenic gas embolism among 4.7 million hospitalizations (2.6/100,000).
In the typical and most severe form, 4% of victims present with cardiac arrest.
Cerebral arterial gas embolism is the major case of death from diving accidents.
In patients undergoing cardiac surgery or a procedure involving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), an estimated 1% to 3% experience a new stroke.
Air embolism occurs in about 0.2% to 0.3% of coronary catheterizations. It is more common among trainees doing percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty.

The incidence of air embolism following percutaneous transthoracic lung biopsy (PTLB) was 0.08%. Risk factors for air embolism included the presence of an underlying disease, the use of a ≥19-gauge needle, and coronary or intracranial air embolism.
Arterial gas embolism can occur via several mechanisms: transpulmonary entry (decompression barotrauma), intracardiac shunt (cardiac septal defect), or direct entry of air into the arterial system:

Decompression barotrauma: Rapid termination of an underwater dive, high-altitude flight, space vehicle excursion, or any other event resulting in a rapid decline in ambient air pressure; expanding gas stretches and ruptures alveoli/alveolar capillaries (pulmonary barotrauma) allowing alveolar gas to enter the arterial circulation.

Direct entry: Lung injury (pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax), alveolar rupture or any procedure that involves incision of a vascular bed in the presence of a hydrostatic pressure gradient favoring entry of gas into the vasculature.

Intracardiac shunt: Migration of venous gas emboli through a pre-existing right to left shunt (septal defect, patent foramen ovale or pulmonary arteriovenous malformation) leading to the entry of gas into arterial circulation (paradoxical emobolization of air).
The fatal dose of air embolism is theorized to be 3 to 5 cc/kg. However, as little as 0.05 cc of air is enough to cause cerebral ischemia if allowed to enter the cerebral arterial tree.

Surgical procedures with the highest risk of arterial gas embolization: Craniotomy performed in the sitting position, cesarean section, hip replacement, and any procedure involving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO).

Decompression associated arterial gas embolism occurs via numerous processes. During ascension, the reduction in ambient pressure results in a decrease in partial pressure of various gases in the vasculature. This reduction in partial pressure allows gas (especially nitrogen) to come out of solution and form bubbles according to Boyle’s Law. These bubbles may form directly in the arterial circulation or the expansion of alveoli can rupture the alveolar capillaries (decompression barotrauma) allowing gas entry into the arterial circulation.

Gas bubbles, on average 30 to 60 micrometers in diameter, migrate into small arteries resulting in reduced distal perfusion and subsequent ischemia. An inflammatory response to the gas bubble also results in cellular damage and cerebral edema from capillary leak.
Coronary or cerebral arteries gas emobolism can be fatal due to the sensitivity of these tissues to even short periods of decreased perfusion and hypoxia.
Hemodynamic complications of air embolism include decreased mean arterial pressure, decreased cardiac output, increased pulmonary artery resistance and pressure, and myocardial ischemia.
Embolization of gas bubbles into the coronary arteries can cause myocardial ischemia/infarction, arrhythmia, myocardial suppression and even cardiac arrest depending on the amount of gas embolized.
Distribution of small gas bubbles into the skeletal muscles or viscera is usually well tolerated without significant residual effects.

Smaller bubbles that do not occlude vessels may still cause transient cerebral or coronary ischemia, endothelial damage, and activation of an inflammatory response, which can still cause secondary ischemia.
The presence of a patent foramen ovale (PFO) increases the risk for arterial air embolism in patients with risk factors for venous air embolism.
Cardiac surgery and any procedure involving ECMO can result in periods of cerebral hypoperfusion, as well as the risk of arterial gas embolism.
Pulmonary complications of air embolism include hypoxia, hypercarbia, pulmonary edema, and bronchoconstriction.
Ischemic end-organ damage may affect brain, spinal cord, heart, kideys, spleen, gastrointestinal tract and skin.

Diagnosis of arterial gas embolism is based primarily on clinical history based on the temporal relation between initial symptoms and an invasive procedure. Patients presenting with typical symptoms of cerebrovascular or coronary ischemia during the intraoperative or perioperative period of a high risk surgical procedure or after a recent underwater dive should be considered for this diagnosis. C

Brain CT is the best initial modality for evaluation of cerebral arterial gas embolism to demonstrate focal ischemia. CT should be followed by diffusion-weighted brain MRI to assess the extent of cerebral injury. C
Quantitative EEG can detect evidence of cerebral arterial gas embolism and can be used to determine improvement during hyperbaric oxygen therapy. C
Coronary arterial gas embolism is suggested by clinical and ECG findings suggesting myocardial ischemia or infarction. C
Echocardiogram can rarely evidence gas within the cardiac chambers, or a PFO which increases the risk of arterial air embolization. C

list.listitem: High index of suspicion based on the direct temporal relation between the initial symptoms and procedures/events as mentioned: (1) cardiac, pulmonary, otolaryngologic, orthopedic or neurosurgical procedure; (2) barotrauma or underwater dive; (3) central venous catheter placement; or (4) penetrating chest trauma.
Signs and symptoms of presentation depend on the initial oragan-system involved.

A classic presentation would be an underwater-diver who develops loss of consciousness, altered mental status, hemipareris, seizure, or cardiac symptoms including chest pain, dyspnea, within minutes of surfacing.

The most severe and classic presentation is loss of consciousness and cardiac arrest, seen in 4% of patients. Any cardiac or focal neurologic symptoms in the correct context can indicate a coronary or cerebral arterial gas embolic event, respectively. Diagnosis in post-operative patients can be complicated by residual effects of anesthesia or adverse responses to anesthesia, which can resemble the effects of cerebral arterial gas embolization.

Symptoms of arterial gas embolism may include dyspnea, sudden inspiration, or “gasp reflex,” dizziness or lightheadedness, chest pain, and an “impending sense of doom.” In less severe cases, the initial symptoms can be minimal and easily missed.

Physical exam findings may include tachypnea, wheezing, rales and respiratory distrss in patients with comorbid venous air embolism. Encephalopathy or new focal neurologic deficit can be seen with cerebral involvement. Tachycardia, hypotension, jugular venous distention or shock can be seen with coronary artery air embolism. Livedo reticularis or retinal artery bubbles can be seen with involvement of the skin and ocular vessels respectively.

The most common manifestation of cerebral arterial gas embolism is a sudden change in sensorium. Cerebral arterial gas embolism can manifest as the sudden development of focal neurologic symptoms or global neurologic dysfunction. In one study, the initial neurologic manifestations of a cerebral air embolism included impaired consciousness (70%), focal motor deficits (60%), seizures (11%), visual disturbances (10%), dysarthria or aphasia (5%), and vertigo (5%).

Alteration in respiratory of circulatory function as a consequence of cerebral arterial gas embolism can manifest as decreased respiratory rate, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, circulatory failure, cardiac arrhythmias, or arrest. In one study involving both venous and arterial cerebral air emboli, 26% manifested hemodynamic disturbances and 23% had respiratory disturbances, with 51% requiring mechanical ventilation.
In post-operative patients, impaired consciousness or difficulty recovering from anesthesia can be the presenting symptom of cerebral arterial gas embolism.

Coronary arterial gas embolism can manifest similar to a typical thromboembolic myocardial infarction, characterized by typical ECG changes (ST elevation or depression, T-wave inversions), arrhythmias, and cardiac arrest.

The diagnosis of arterial gas embolism is often clinical. There is no single specific lab test to accurately diagnose arterial gas embolism. Laboratory tests should be tailored to the presenting signs/symptoms and the organ-sytem involved.
Initial laboratory tests include CBC, CK and ABG. Imaging tests including CT scan, MRI, and echocardiogram can help aid the diagnosis.

Hemoconcentration, suggested by an elevated hematocrit, may sometimes be seen in cases of arterial gas embolism, possibly due to extravascular shifts of fluids into injured tissues. This is, however, a nonspecific finding.
Elevation in CK has been observed in patients with diving-associated gas embolism.
ABG may show evidence of hypoxemia, hypercarbia or elevated A-a gradient in patients with comorbid venous air embolism.
Initial imaging studies to be considered include chest X-ray, CT of the chest, CT of the head, transthoracic echocardiogram and transcranial doppler ultrasound.
Plain radiographs, which can visualize large amounts of intravascular air,particularly in patients with comorbid venous air embolism.

In some cases, cerebral arterial gas embolism can be distinguished from cerebral infarct or hemorrhage on CT scan, although the changes seen with arterial gas embolism are subtle and typically not well visualized. The typical findings on CT scan including pneumocephalus and cerebral edema, which may be seen with or without arterial infarction. Air may sometimes also be seen in the subarachnoid spaces.

CT scan may not be effective if not performed immediately after the embolic event because air is quickly resorbed from the vasculature into tissues. Therefore, a brain CT scan should be performed immediately as soon as cerebral arterial gas embolism is suspected.

After a diagnosis of cerebral arterial gas embolism is suggested by CT scan, an MRI should be performed to evaluate the extent of cerebral injury. Diffusion-weighted MRI may not show signs of ischemia if performed immediately after the event, but findings of multiple restricted diffusion areas in a gyriform pattern, or in watershed areas with decompression barotrauma, have been associated with cerebral arterial gas embolism.
Gas bubbles can sometimes be detected on retinal exam, but their absence does not rule-out cerebral arterial gas embolism.

In a pig model, quantitative EEG (qEEG) was able to demonstrate changes in brain function after experiencing cerebral arterial gas embolism and was used to monitor recovery after appropriate treatment. The investigators believed that EEG may be used to measure treatment outcomes but did not comment on the applicability of qEEG to initial diagnosis and evaluation.

Echocardiogram may reveal air in right ventricle; one may also see right ventricular dilation from pulmonary artery hypertension. PFO may also been seen. In one study of 230 divers PFO was shown to increase the risk of symptoms of arterial embolization, with larger PFO size correlated with incremental risk.
ECG may reveal tachycardia, peaked P-waves, ST-segment or T-wave changes, and other signs of acute MI.

Diagnosis is primarily based on clinical suspicion and patient history, particularly if neurologic or cardiac symptoms present shortly after a patient undergoes a rapid change in ambient pressure or an invasive surgical procedure.

Large-volume air emboli may cause cardiovascular collapse, end-organ ischemia including brain and spinal cord, or even death. A severe air embolus may mimic a CVA, acute MI, or even a pulmonary thromboemboli.
Tests that can support the diagnosis of cerebral arterial gas embolism include CT scan, MRI and EEG.
ECG changes typical of ischemia or infarction can support the diagnosis of coronary arterial gas embolism.

Echocardiography can show changes in contractility which may suggest coronary arterial gas embolism; PFO increases risk of arterial air embolization and presence of air within the cardiac chambers is rare, but pathognomonic for gas embolization in the presence of correlating symptoms.
Initial management involves stabilization of the patient, cardio-pulmonary support as needed, and then initiation of the diagnostic workup.
The primary goals of treatment are to stabilize the patient, prevent further air embolization, initiate supportive care, and restore pre-embolus physiology. C
The principles of treatment of arterial gas embolism should focus on:1) Maintaining hemodynamic stability,2) Terminating the source of air,3) Decreasing the size of air bubble.
The patient should initially be placed on maximum supplemental oxygen and placed in the supine position. The Trendelenburg position should be avoided as this can aggravate cerebral edema. C
Hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) is the treatment of choice for arterial gas embolism and treatment should be initiated as soon as possible. C
In patients with diving-associated arterial gas embolism, recompression should be used in conjunction with HBO therapy. C
Infusion, anticoagulant, corticosteroid, and lidocaine are controversial therapies for cerebral arterial gas embolism and are currently not officially recommended. C

The use of anticoagulant therapy is currently not recommended, although there is some evidence that heparin may be beneficial. The counterargument is the possibility of hemorrhagic conversion in already infarcted tissue.

The use of corticosteroids to reduce brain edema is also controversial. Arterial air embolism results in cytotoxic brain edema, which usually does not respond to corticosteroids; studies have reported aggravation of ischemic insult with corticosteroids use.

Lidocaine therapy has been proposed as a treatment for cerebral arterial gas embolism. However, a recent study showed no neuroprotective effects of lidocaine, including no difference in self-rating of memory function or length of ICU or hospital stay.
Gas embolism during cardiac catheterization is often treated with intracoronary vasodilators (i.e., nicardipine, nitroglycerine).

Stabilize the patient and attempt to prevent further embolization and identify the cause. Supplemental oxygen at the highest available concentrations should be administered to treat hypoxia and hypoxemia caused by the arterial gas embolus. High concentration oxygen also helps decrease the bubble size by establishing a diffusion gradient favoring the egress of gas from the bubbles.

Place the patient in the supine position, avoiding the Trendelenburg position as this can worsen cerebral edema. The gas bubble’s buoyancy cannot counteract the force of blood flow toward the brain, even in the Trendelenburg position, so it is not useful to place the patient in this position.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBO) is the first-line treatment of choice for arterial gas embolism. HBO decreases the size of gas bubbles in the vasculature and increases the amount of oxygen dissolved in blood plasma, thereby improving oxygen diffusion into tissues. Initiation of HBO within 3 h of cerebral arterial gas embolism was shown in a small study to significantly improve neurologic recovery, as compared with those whose treatment was delayed between 9 and 20 hours. Although studies have stressed the importance of initiating HBO therapy early, these same studies have not produced enough data to determine recommendations for duration of treatment.
Recompression therapy in conjunction with HBO is first line therapy in patients with suspected decompression pathophysiology. A commonly used recompression protocol is the U.S. Navy Treatment Table.

Recompression therapy with adjuvant NSAID therapy or use of Heliox (helium and oxygen) treatment tables have been tested. A 2012 Cochrane review concluded that both therapies may be justified as an RCT for both adjuvant therapies showed a reduction in the number of recompressions required; however no difference in the odds of recover was noted in either.

There is some evidence that gas embolism can lead to hemoconcentration from extravasation of gases into tissues, which can lead to increased blood viscosity when there is already decreased microvascular circulation. Therefore, some advocate hemodilution to a hematocrit of 30%.

Some advocate the use of colloid over crystalloid solutions due to the possibility of crystalloid worsening cerebral edema. Additionally, as the goal is normovolemia, it is recommended that CVP should be maintained at 12 mmHg and urine output at 1 to 2 mL/kg/h.
Patients with known complex congenital heart defects (with intra-cardiac shunts) should have micron filters used on occasions when they require intravenous access.
There is little evidence to support the routine practice of percutaneous closure of patent foramen ovale in subjects (especially divers) with recurrent paradoxical embolism.

Seizures resulting from cerebral arterial gas embolism may be treated with barbiturates if they do not respond to benzodiazepines. Barbiturates have been shown to decrease cerebral oxygen consumption, intracranial pressure, free-radical production, and release of catecholamines.
In patients experiencing intraoperative stroke, significant neurocognitive deficits remaining in 30% to 65% of patients. These deficits may remain after at least 5 years in 42% of these patients.B

In one study of a small number of patients with cerebral arterial gas embolism, approximately 39% of patients had a good outcome with total neurologic recovery, whereas 61% had a poor outcome including lasting neurologic deficits and death. A shorter time period before initiation of hyperbaric oxygen therapy correlated with a better outcome.B
A prospective cohort study found that increasing age (OR 1.07/year), Babinski sign (OR 6.6), and acute kidney failure (OR 8.1) were predictors of mortality at 1 year.
